doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

chapter: Kent State and the Eastman job
title: How Dobbins was hired at Eastman
summary: Ted Price and Clark Terry both recommended Dobbins when Chuck Mangione's teaching post opened under Rayburn Wright.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: And I think it was about ’71, maybe ’72, no I think it was ’71, that Chuck Mangione, he had a really big commercial success with this record that he did with the Rochester Philharmonic called “Friends and Love.” And he had been teaching here as an instructor at the time that Ray came up from Radio City in New York and decided to move to Rochester and start a — well mostly a jazz writing curriculum. Chuck had been doing improvisation and they had a big band here, and so Ray came to do a whole sequence of writing courses. And around ’71 here when Chuck had this big success, he decided to go out and make a career for himself as a performer and end his teaching duties here. So the position opened up. And right around the time the position opened up, what usually happens in the searches, two of the people that Ray talked to, to see if they knew of anybody that they thought would be good for this job were this music critic, Ted Price, and he just happened to have as a guest soloist with the Eastman Jazz Ensemble right then, Clark Terry. So he asked both of these guys, you know, if they thought they knew anybody that would be good for this job. And both of them said right away, Bill Dobbins.

The planets aligned for you. That’s interesting because now I was speculating, if you were to go on and do something else or retire or whatever, I think there’d be a lot of applicants for your position.

Well I’m sure, yeah. I feel really fortunate that I was able to get this position at a time when having any kind of an advanced degree at all was fine. I don’t think I’d been here more than fifteen years when everything had already reached the point that people looking for any kind of serious job in college teaching, even if it was in a jazz program, a doctorate was expected.

You know I had a similar experience at SUNY Fredonia in the music department. There was no jazz so to speak, but it was all student initiative. But there was something fantastic about that, that we were driven. We thought we were special. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
